thinking: Thinking Process: Evaluating 'Oh Victoria, Victoria!' by Paul Strangio. We analyze Victoria's political climate leading up to the November 2026 election, featuring deep public disillusionment with major parties, rising anti-establishment sentiment, and historical echoes. Stated claim: a standard democratic transition or ordinary electoral swing. Ground reality: a profound systemic breakdown and voter alienation driven by decades of institutional negligence, corruption scandals (CFMEU), and political exhaustion. We will compute granular forces, coordinate offsets, and apply the strict SON JSON schema.
subject: Oh Victoria, Victoria! • Paul Strangio
posts:
As Victoria heads toward an uneasy November election, Paul Strangio examines a deep statewide mood of fury, sullenness, and impending dread.
Evidence: voter disillusionment, three-party shift, historical echoes
#Aletheia #Victoria #AusPol

Stated Claim: Victorian politics is experiencing a routine multi-party electoral realignment driven by normal voter dissatisfaction.
Stated Judgement: (+0.5, 0.0) — Good Preference

Ground Reality: Chronic institutional decay, corruption scandals, and policy failure have produced a systemic crisis of faith in major parties.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.75, -0.85) — Greater Evil

Verdict: FAIL — The Path of Deception.
Voters face a profound structural crisis masked as routine electoral fatigue.

Integrity: Severe Deception (Hypocrisy: 6.2, z: 2)

Sub-Audits Breakdown:
- Labor Incumbency: FAIL (-0.80, -0.90) — Scandals and policy fatigue.
- Liberal Opposition: FAIL (-0.70, -0.80) — Chronic internal dysfunction.
With the state facing an unusual three-and-a-half-party contest and collapsing primary votes for major parties, Victorians confront an unprecedented political vacuum.

The Bright Side:
Voters are breaking free from a stagnant two-party duopoly, opening space for alternative political voices.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Confusing a terminal institutional crisis (WHO/Metaphysical plane) with a simple electoral swing (WHAT/Possible plane).

Social Physics Analysis:
Political elites ran a smart selfish loop, trading long-term institutional health for short-term control, while projecting blame onto external crises.

The Trajectory: The Path of Deception.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Greater Evil. Stated democratic stability masks deep extraction.

The Unavoidable Truth: Public fury reflects genuine institutional betrayal rather than temporary bad mood.

The Unavoidable Lie: Major parties can restore trust through superficial campaign resets.

Alethekanon:
Surface-level electoral analysis obscures a deeper structural rot in Victorian governance. Institutional exhaustion cannot be cured by ballot-box musical chairs.

Awwthekanon:
It is heartbreaking to watch communities lose all faith in the systems meant to serve them, sliding into cynicism and despair.

Brothekanon:
Everyone's just sick of the same old mess. People want a fresh start, but the options look pretty grim.

Spirithekanon:
"The people are exhausted and disheartened, like sheep without a shepherd." Matthew 9:36 PASS
When leaders fail the public trust, communities are left wandering in political despair.

Oh Victoria, Victoria! • Paul Strangio

A kind of dread hangs over the state as the November election approaches

Actual Article Body:
Menu

A kind of dread hangs over the state as the November election approaches

Paul Strangio 2 October 2026 2541 words

Trouble ahead: Victoria’s then premier Daniel Andrews and his successor Jacinta Allan inspecting one of Labor’s Big Build projects following the late-2020 Covid lockdown. Asanka Ratnayake/ Getty Images

When Victorians head to the polls on the last Saturday of next month, all the indications are that they will usher in that relatively rare thing — a change of state government. The twelve-year-old Labor administration, led by the recently installed Ben Carroll, is widely predicted to be unsentimentally flung from office.

That expectation might typically engender anticipation of a fresh beginning and reinvigoration. Yet the political atmosphere in Victoria is a long way from optimism. If the mood of the state’s citizens were to be summed up, it would be a mixture of fury, sullenness and despair overlaid with an element of impending dread.

All elections are, of course, distinctive. But as a longtime observer of Victorian politics, I have to say this one feels strikingly uncommon, at least in living memory, at two levels. First, as opinion polls consistently show, this is a genuine three-party contest, or perhaps more accurately three and a half: Labor versus the Coalition versus Pauline Hanson’s One Nation, with the Greens representing the extra half. And second, the public’s disenchantment with the choices on offer is unusually intense.

The disillusionent is especially directed towards the major parties, Labor and Liberal. According to the polls, neither can be confident of winning 30 per cent of the primary vote. The anger at incumbent Labor is particularly fierce: very few can objectively believe it deserves another term.

In fact, you need to go a long way back to find an election in which the party holding office was so discredited in the eyes of voters. The nearest approximation is Labor at the end of the Cain–Kirner era in the early 1990s when, with the state battered by economic recession and roiled by industrial strife, the ALP was brutally and effectively tarred as the “Guilty Party” in Liberal Party advertising.

And yet this ire hasn’t sent voters into the arms of the Liberal Party. Years of internecine squabbling, leadership chaos and policy negligence have created abiding distrust of the Liberals as a viable alternative government. By way of contrast, One Nation, a party that historically has attracted derisory levels of support in Victoria, is generating enthusiasm within sections of the electorate. But that seems driven more by a blow-everything-up nihilism than a genuine conviction that the party represents a constructive option for running the state.

In short, what we have in Victoria is a powerful pox-on-all-houses sentiment. Voters feel cheated.

How unprecedented is this? Interestingly, in some ways, it resonates with the patterns of Victorian state politics that prevailed during large parts of the first half of the twentieth century. The state’s politics during that period were peculiarly retrograde compared to most of the other states, mainly because of its triangular party system (Labor versus Liberal — or its earlier iterations — versus Country Party), which translated into chronic instability, cynical deal-making and unproductive governance. Victorian politics might be said to be in danger of regressing to that ugly past — to a time, long expunged from its citizens’ memory, that doesn’t fit with the state’s self-perception as the nation’s heartland of civilised progressivism.

Putting that awkward scenario aside, this election — which has significant chance of raising One Nation to a share in government — does feel “unVictorian” when measured against the state’s better-known political traditions.
